newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore growth to remain solid - economists.
newsitem.headline: Singapore growth to remain solid - economists.

text.p: Economists said on Tuesday they were more optimistic than the Singapore government on the country's growth rate this year, but both sides said they expected the economy to speed along at a healthy clip.
The government, announcing its latest economic data that confirmed 1996 growth was better than expected, kept to its forecast that growth this year would be between five and seven percent.
However, economists said seven percent was the least Singapore could expect.

"We think the government is slightly on the pessimistic side for growth in 1997. We are forecasting growth of seven percent, the top end of the range," Angus Armstrong, chief economist, Asia, for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, told Reuters.
Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at J.M. Sassoon, said he was likely to revise his growth forecast upwards to 7.5 percent.
The economy grew at 7.0 percent in 1996, the Ministry of Trade and Industry confirmed on Tuesday.

The data reflected a stronger than expected fourth quarter, when the economy grew by 5.8 percent. The finance and business services sector was especially strong, expanding by 10 percent against 6.4 percent in the third quarter.
The construction sector was also robust, growing 13.7 percent in the last quarter to end the full year with an expansion of 18.4 percent.
The manufacturing sector, however, remained weak. It shrank by 0.7 percent in the fourth quarter and grew a mere 3.4 percent over the full year. In 1995, it grew 10 percent.
The manufacturing contraction was largely due to a glut in the world electronics market, bad news for a country whose electronics industry accounts for some 60 percent of non-oil exports.
Singapore's 1996 7.0 percent growth was a slice under the 8.8 percent growth in 1995 and a chunk below 1994's 10.5 percent.
But the economists said confirmation that the electronics industry was recovering should come after the second quarter and they said company order books were already indicating the tide had turned.
Song Seng Wun, economist at HG Asia, said he expected the manufacturing sector to remain soft in the first quarter this year, with growth at one-two percent.
But he said manufacturing should rise 5.0 to 5.5 percent in 1997 and the gross domestic product (GDP) should climb 6.7 percent over the full year.
Liew of JM Sassoon said Singapore's huge disk drive industry could offset weaknesses in semiconductor prices in 1997, one area of uncertainty still facing the electronics industry.
The disk drive industry had been seeing demand outstripping supply in recent months and the outlook for 1997 was positive, industry researchers previously said.

"Semiconductors could hold back output growth but the DRAM (dynamic random access memories) output here is relatively small compared to disk drives. The good performance there should offset weakness in the other," Liew said. Singapore produces about 45 percent of the world's hard disk drives.
Economists said they expected the finance sector, with growth of around eight percent, and construction, booming along in double digits, to lead Singapore's growth again in 1997.

A senior government official told reporters after the new figures were released that the relative slowdown in 1996 cut into productivity growth figures, which dived to 0.7 percent against growth of 3-3.5 percent in the last five to 10 years.
But he said that resulted from companies not releasing workers because they anticipated a pick-up in 1997.
Economists expected productivity to rebound to the three percent range in 1997.
